saint_pick.name: Narcissus of Jerusalem
saint_pick.selection_reason: Eusebius documents Narcissus's story: the miracle of water turned to oil for the Easter vigil lamps, the slander by three men whose oaths of innocence ended in fire, disease and blindness, his retreat into the desert, and his return as a bishop over 100 years old. It is vivid, surprising and early, and he is not a household name.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Roman Martyrology, feast on October 29 (Latin Church). He is also venerated in the Eastern Churches, with the Orthodox feast on August 7.

beats.text: Falsely accused, the old bishop forgave his accusers and left Jerusalem.
beats.scene: An elderly bishop with a white beard and plain early-Christian vestments stands before a small group of men in a stone hall. He raises one hand in a gesture of forgiveness. Their faces are lowered, and the arched windows show a hazy Judean sky.

beats.text: Saint Narcissus of Jerusalem, of Greek origin, born, tradition holds, in the year ninety-nine. He became Jerusalem's thirtieth bishop at eighty or more.
According to Eusebius, at the Easter Vigil he changed water into oil, so every lamp in the church could burn.
beats.scene: Inside a modest early church at night, the aged bishop Narcissus blesses a large clay jar as deacons hold rows of small oil lamps. Warm light falls on the faces of the gathered faithful, and the walls are plain plastered stone.
beats.art_hint: Easter vigil lamps lit in an early church, a bishop blessing a jar of oil; search: Easter vigil lamps icon, oil lamps early church, bishop blessing oil

beats.text: People in his own Christian community accused him of serious wrongs. The charges proved false. He lived in seclusion for several years.
beats.scene: The aged bishop Narcissus walks alone along a rocky path out of the walled city of Jerusalem, carrying a staff. Behind him are ancient stone walls and gates, and ahead of him are quiet Judean hills at dusk.
beats.art_hint: a solitary elderly saint leaving a city for the hills; hermit in the Judean landscape; search: Judean desert icon, hermit saint landscape, Jerusalem walls icon

beats.text: Three bishops governed in his absence. When he returned, the people unanimously asked him to resume his duties.
beats.scene: A crowd of men, women and children in tunics and cloaks gathers at a Jerusalem gate to welcome the returning bishop Narcissus. He is white-haired and leaning on a staff, and the people reach out their hands to him.
beats.art_hint: a bishop welcomed back by the faithful at the gates of Jerusalem; search: return of the bishop icon, Jerusalem gate icon, early Christian community icon

beats.text: Too old to carry it alone, he named Alexander his assistant bishop, and kept serving through constant prayer and calls for unity and peace. His answer to injury was forgiveness, and his gift to the Church was peace.
beats.scene: The aged bishop Narcissus sits in prayer beside the younger bishop Alexander, one hand resting on his shoulder. They are in a simple early-Christian chapel with a lamp burning before them.

script.caption_hook: A bishop past eighty was slandered by his own people. His answer was forgiveness.
script.summary: Saint Narcissus of Jerusalem, an early bishop, was falsely accused, forgave his accusers, lived in seclusion, and returned at the people's request to serve in prayer and peace.

claims.claim: Narcissus of Jerusalem lived from about 99 to about 216 AD and was an early bishop (patriarch) of Jerusalem.
Of Greek origin, he was born in the year 99, according to tradition.
He was at least eighty when he became the thirtieth bishop of Jerusalem.
According to Eusebius, at the Easter Vigil Narcissus changed water into oil to supply all the lamps of the church.
Members of the Christian community made serious allegations against him, which proved false.
He forgave his accusers and left Jerusalem to live in seclusion for several years.
Three bishops governed the See of Jerusalem in succession during his absence.
On his return the people unanimously asked him to resume his episcopal duties.
Because of his extreme age and the weight of his duties, he made Alexander of Jerusalem his coadjutor bishop.
He continued to serve through constant prayer and exhortations to the faithful for unity and peace.
He is venerated in the Roman Catholic Church on October 29.

story: Saint Narcissus of Jerusalem lived to be 116 years old, and the Church remembers him above all as a man whose old age was spiritually strong. His name is the same as that of the youth in Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection. The saint had nothing else in common with him. The old Italian lives of the saints note that he was the opposite of that figure: humble, devoted to others, and vigorous in body and mind to the end.

He was born around the year 96, though some sources say 99. The sources agree that he was not of Jewish family. Tradition holds that he was of Greek origin. He came into the world when the ruins left by the Roman destruction of Jerusalem, under Titus, were still fresh. Over the course of his long life he watched the city slowly rise again and fill with people. It came to hold a large Christian community alongside its Jewish neighbors.

He was almost a hundred years old when he was chosen as the thirtieth bishop of Jerusalem. The Catholic sources say he was chosen for his virtue more than for his age. He did not treat the office as an honor to rest in. He governed for many years and with firmness. He presided over a council of the bishops of Palestine, held at Caesarea, which decided that Easter should always be kept on a Sunday. The Roman Martyrology records that he stood in full agreement with Pope Saint Victor on this, and that the mystery of the Lord's Resurrection could only be celebrated on a Sunday.

One miracle of note is attributed to him, and it comes to us through the historian Eusebius. On the night of Easter, the oil for the church's lamps ran out and the wicks stood dry. Narcissus is said to have changed water into oil, so that the lamps could be lit for the Vigil. This is the Church's tradition of what happened, handed down by Eusebius, and not an event we can confirm from other records.

Narcissus was a stern bishop. He wanted the people around him to be honest, humble and good, and his firmness troubled those who were corrupt. Some of them struck back with a grave accusation against him, which they backed with solemn oaths. History does not tell us what the charge was. It does tell us that it was false. Not everyone believed it, but to spare the Church scandal, the aged bishop left Jerusalem, though he was innocent. Tradition holds that he withdrew to the desert to live in seclusion. He is also remembered as having forgiven his accusers.

According to the old account, those who had sworn falsely were struck by terrible punishments, until one of them confessed the lie. By then, Narcissus was thought to be dead. Two successors were elected one after the other. When the second died, Narcissus reappeared in Jerusalem, and the faithful led him back to his bishop's chair with great honor.

He was far too old to carry the work alone, so he took a coadjutor, Alexander, who later became a saint himself. The Italian reference describes this as the first such arrangement in the history of the episcopate, a custom that continues today. Narcissus went on serving his flock and others beyond it through constant prayer and urging the faithful toward unity and peace.

The last word we have of him is in a letter from Alexander. As the Italian source gives it, the letter says that Narcissus sends his greetings, that he has completed one hundred and sixteen years, and that he urges the faithful, as Alexander does, to keep concord. His feast is celebrated in the Roman Catholic Church on October 29, and in the Eastern Orthodox Church on August 7. His emblem is the pastoral staff. His long life shows holiness that accepts an injustice without bitterness and keeps working for peace.

issues: Beat 'who': 'a Greek born' was awkward and 'its thirtieth bishop' had no clear antecedent in the narration. Changed to 'of Greek origin, born, tradition holds, in the year ninety-nine' and 'Jerusalem's thirtieth bishop'. The tradition framing is kept.
Beat 'story' (accusations): the opening 'Then' implied a chronological order that the source does not give. Removed it.

Beat 'turn': the closing line 'his gift to the Church was peace' is devotional interpretation. It rests on the sourced 'exhortations for unity and peace' but is not stated in the source. Left in as a reflection, and flagged for the approver.

The source's dates are internally strained. Born 99 and at least 80 at his episcopate would make him well over 100 at death in c. 216. The script already marks the birth year as 'tradition holds', which is acceptable. The miracle is attributed to Eusebius, which is correct.
The map (Jerusalem, 31.7683, 35.2137), feast date October 29, 'Saint' title and martyr:false all check out against the source. Word count is about 137, within the 125-145 range.
factcheck.reviewer_note: The source is a single Wikipedia article, and the birth year 99 and death year 216 would imply an age over 115. Consider softening the dates on screen, and check that the closing line about 'his gift to the Church was peace' is acceptable as reflection.

STORY beat said three bishops governed in his absence (Wikipedia). The Catholic reference says he was thought dead and two successors were elected, and he returned when the second died. Rewrote the beat to the Catholic version. 'The people unanimously asked him' came from Wikipedia only and was replaced with 'the faithful restored him with honor'.
Caption hook said 'past eighty', which no longer matches the corrected age. Reworded.
Story paragraph: 'in the year 70' for the destruction under Titus is not in the sources. Removed.
Story paragraph: 'One miracle is attributed to him' conflicts with Wikipedia, which says Eusebius records many miracles and one of note. Changed to 'One miracle of note'.
Claims list updated to match the corrected beats.

recheck.reviewer_note: Sources disagree on Narcissus's birth year (96 vs 99), his age at election (nearly 100 vs 80+) and the number of successors (two vs three); I followed the Catholic reference. es.name: San Narciso de Jerusalén
es.hook: Un obispo de más de ochenta años fue calumniado por los suyos. Su respuesta fue el perdón.
es.summary: San Narciso de Jerusalén, un obispo de los primeros tiempos, fue acusado falsamente, perdonó a sus acusadores, vivió en retiro y regresó a petición del pueblo para servir en la oración y la paz.
story: San Narciso de Jerusalén vivió hasta los 116 años, y la Iglesia lo recuerda sobre todo como un hombre cuya vejez fue espiritualmente fuerte. Su nombre es el mismo que el del joven de la mitología griega que se enamoró de su propio reflejo. El santo no tuvo nada más en común con él. Las antiguas vidas de santos italianas señalan que fue lo contrario de aquel personaje: humilde, entregado a los demás y vigoroso en cuerpo y mente hasta el final.

Nació hacia el año 96, aunque algunas fuentes dicen 99. Las fuentes coinciden en que no era de familia judía. Según la tradición, era de origen griego. Vino al mundo cuando aún estaban frescas las ruinas dejadas por la destrucción romana de Jerusalén bajo Tito. A lo largo de su larga vida vio cómo la ciudad se reconstruía poco a poco y se llenaba de gente. Llegó a tener una numerosa comunidad cristiana junto a sus vecinos judíos.

Tenía casi cien años cuando fue elegido trigésimo obispo de Jerusalén. Las fuentes católicas dicen que fue elegido por su virtud más que por su edad. No consideró el cargo como un honor para descansar. Gobernó durante muchos años con firmeza. Presidió un concilio de obispos de Palestina, celebrado en Cesarea, que decidió que la Pascua debía celebrarse siempre en domingo. El Martirologio Romano registra que estuvo plenamente de acuerdo en esto con el papa San Víctor, y que el misterio de la Resurrección del Señor solo podía celebrarse en domingo.

Se le atribuye un milagro notable, que nos llega a través del historiador Eusebio. En la noche de Pascua se acabó el aceite de las lámparas de la iglesia y las mechas quedaron secas. Se dice que Narciso convirtió agua en aceite, para que las lámparas pudieran encenderse durante la Vigilia. Esta es la tradición de la Iglesia sobre lo sucedido, transmitida por Eusebio, y no un hecho que podamos confirmar con otros documentos.

Narciso era un obispo severo. Quería que las personas a su alrededor fueran honradas, humildes y buenas, y su firmeza incomodaba a los corruptos. Algunos de ellos contraatacaron con una grave acusación contra él, que respaldaron con juramentos solemnes. La historia no nos dice cuál era la acusación. Sí nos dice que era falsa. No todos la creyeron, pero para evitar un escándalo a la Iglesia, el anciano obispo abandonó Jerusalén, aunque era inocente. Según la tradición, se retiró al desierto para vivir en soledad. También se le recuerda por haber perdonado a sus acusadores.

Según el antiguo relato, quienes habían jurado en falso sufrieron terribles castigos, hasta que uno de ellos confesó la mentira. Para entonces, se creía que Narciso había muerto. Se eligieron dos sucesores, uno tras otro. Cuando murió el segundo, Narciso reapareció en Jerusalén, y los fieles lo llevaron de vuelta a su cátedra episcopal con gran honor.

Era demasiado anciano para cargar solo con la labor, así que tomó como coadjutor a Alejandro, que más tarde también llegó a ser santo. La referencia italiana describe esto como el primer caso de este tipo en la historia del episcopado, una costumbre que continúa hoy. Narciso siguió sirviendo a su rebaño y a otros más allá de él mediante la oración constante y exhortando a los fieles a la unidad y la paz.

La última noticia que tenemos de él está en una carta de Alejandro. Según la fuente italiana, la carta dice que Narciso envía sus saludos, que ha cumplido ciento dieciséis años y que exhorta a los fieles, como lo hace Alejandro, a mantener la concordia. Su fiesta se celebra en la Iglesia católica romana el 29 de octubre, y en la Iglesia ortodoxa oriental el 7 de agosto. Su emblema es el báculo pastoral. Su larga vida muestra una santidad que acepta la injusticia sin amargura y que sigue trabajando por la paz.
